projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Singleton was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Robert J. Singleton. Mr. Singleton served in the U.S. Army with the 87th Infantry Division, 335th Field Artillery Battalion. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Singleton's home in North Royalton, Ohio, on July 18th, 2002. Bob was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Late in 1942. Got out in 1946. And we came back; the war was still on. As a matter of fact, we left Le Havre, France, 4th of July 1945 at 12 o'clock noon, and it's a day I'll never forget. So we came home with -- we were going to the Pacific. And we came home, and it was the division -- and we went to Fort Benning, Georgia. And while we were there, they dropped the bomb, the 27th of August. And they didn't know what was happening until -- because they hadn't invaded Japan proper yet because all the war in the Pacific was on somebody else's property. It wasn't on Japan. And they didn't know what was going to happen once -- they were going to be fighting the civilians and kids and everything else. It's like we were in Germany. So once they sent troops in and they found out there wasn't going to be no problems, then they started discharging us. They sent me up to Camp Edderburg, Pennsylvania -- not -- Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania. And the war was never declared over at that time, and so I was in until January of '46. And the war not being declared, two or three of us were in the inactive reserves. So I was in the reserve for three years, which I didn't have to be. It was inactive. And I got two discharges -- one from World War II and one from Reserves. So I had six years of service time, but three of them was inactive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Drafted, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: 18. See, there was two drafts. A lot of people don't know. There was the first draft in 1940, which I was 21 years old. And of course I wasn't 21 at that time. I was in -- in school, and then they lowered the draft to 18. And I would say the bulk of the people in World War II was from 18 years old and up. Because of -- there was a mass, you know, between 18 and 21, and so our division was called the baby division. And every one of them in some wartime division was loaded with kids my age and guys out of college and that, so -- but there was old-timers. And, as a matter of fact, our first sergeant was from World War I, so. And some of the officers even, they never seen no combat, and they were just as green as we were, so. And we had some West Pointers, and so that's basically as far as the history of the division.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you about 16, 17 when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: 1941, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, real well. As a matter of fact, I was born and raised in Youngstown. And I just so happened to go down there for the weekend to see a girlfriend or something, and we went to somebody's house, and the girl's father said they bombed Pearl Harbor. "Where is Pearl Harbor?" Nobody knew where it was at. But a lot of kids that I knew, older kids, they were in the National Guard, which was a 37th Division. And a lot of those guys -- I think the 37th Division -- I think spent more time overseas than anybody. They got called up in 1940. They got called up before then, dropping the -- I mean, the Pearl Harbor attack. And they were over in the islands there like four and a half years, I think, and a lot of the guys I knew got killed. They were, you know -- they were 18 years old. They joined a guard, and they were in the service and were -- most of us younger kids. We got caught in the 18-year-old draft, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing that news that day about the Japanese attack?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It shocked everybody. Nobody knew anything about it, and everybody tried to get maps. And of course all we had was the radio in those days, and a lot of people didn't even have radios, you know, and half of them didn't work. Right out of the depression, you know. And everybody headed for home and, you know, it was a shock. And then little by little it got worse where they thought they would invade West Coast and pretty tight and a little scary. And of course -- of course today it's a little bit different because if you lived on the coast, it wasn't too bad. When you lived in the interior place, I guess, even the East Coast, and of course some of the people were involved at that time with Europe because the war was going on over there. And the only thing that we had going over was ships hauling material. And if you remember correctly or from history that we were not involved in that war other than hauling supplies over to England. And I know when we were going over ourself, we had a submarine scare when we went overseas ourself right out of New York -- first day out of New York.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Stopped and -- what the hell was this? It's submarines out there, and so they had nothing to do. But back to 1941 -- but this was two years later.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about -- you went in in '42. What can you tell me about the training?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well, went up to Camp Perry here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Their first shock of the Army was people from here usually went to Perry or Fort Hayes. And people that was drafted before me and they got up to Perry, and if they were there -- if they were there on Friday, they weren't going to be shipped out until Monday, and their parents or girlfriends could go up to visit them. And it just so happened that I got drafted on a Thursday and went up there on a Thursday. I was drafted -- I was drafted a month before there but went up there. And actually, I -- before I got that far, I had a chance of -- people don't realize that the Navy and the Marines was draftees, too. And when I went to -- inducted 30 days before I left, physically fit. I had a mechanical background, so they asked me if I wanted to go in the Marines first. It just so happens some young fellow was working with me, a friend of mine, he went into the Marines and four months later he got killed. Four months. And I wasn't too happy. If they would have said, go to the Marines, fine. But then they said, "You got a mechanical background. Do you want to be a machinist mate in the Navy?" And I said, "No. I'm not too happy about the Navy." I went in the Army. A lot of people don't know that. They think the Navy and Marines was all volunteers, and it wasn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you were drafted, you actually had the choice of --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: At that time because I was physically fit, and everybody didn't. If somebody had a handicap maybe or certain things and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They had to put --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And I had the mechanical background from working in the machine shop. And so it depended how they needed them, too. And if you didn't make no decision, they made it for you. You went to the Army. So I went up to Camp Perry on a Thursday. And come Saturday afternoon they started to call out some names. And they said, if your name is not called, you'll be here for the weekend. My name was not called. So a real snowy day, come Sunday -- and I called my parents, my brother. And they said they'd be up Sunday. So Saturday night somewhere in the middle of the night some guy come and woke me up, and he says, "You didn't answer your name." I says, "You didn't call it." And he said, "Well, we had another list of -- and your name was called." And he said, "Get your stuff together." And this was 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning. "Get your stuff together and you're shipping out." Well, you know, he didn't know from beans from nothing. You did -- everybody was a corporal or something, and they were like a general. I mean, you didn't know anything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So they hauled us over to some rec room, locked us in there, MPs at the door, just like we were prisoners. And the post headquarters was right across the street. I'm looking out the window. I see my mother, brother drive up there. And I told the MP, I says, "That's my parents out there." "You're not going out." So pretty soon I see my brother coming out, and he's shaking his hand. And we sat there probably about o'clock Sunday afternoon in that building. And I said, "What the hell; my parents are right across the street. Can't I get out?" "No." So that night we got on the train. Didn't know where the hell we were going. Shades pulled like we were special troops or something. Didn't know nothing. I had a uniform and didn't know how to put it on even.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So we ended up -- first sign of -- of course in those days everything was railroad. Railroad and the passenger -- not passenger trains, but war materials with tanks or anything like that had -- had priority.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And the passenger trains would pull off on the side to leave them go by, and you'd see tanks going by and trucks and everything. So the first time we knew anyplace we was at, the blinds are down all night long. And I saw a sign, "Memphis, Tennessee." Hell, I'd never been to Memphis, Tennessee. Never wanted to go to Memphis, Tennessee. So we pulled out from there. We went down the road a bit, and we stopped by an air base. And, oh, Christ, we think we're in the air corp, you know. We were on the side. We didn't know it. So we went down to a town called Grenada, Mississippi, right in the middle of a cotton belt, and this was a temporary camp, fire paper shacks, and they built it for World War II. Knocked down the cotton fields.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And it just so happened the fellows that were going to train us was coming out of Fort Rucker, Alabama, which was an 87th Division, and these guys were all corporals or that. And they moved them up, and there's a category for the 87th Division with officers and that. And this is -- we was in Camp McKay, Mississippi, for the best part of six months, I guess. And the towns -- once you did go to town, there was nothing there. One movie. Nothing to drink. All dry, you know. And one thing that scared us a little bit is one of the old soldiers asked me one day -- he said, "Where are you from?" I told him. He said -- I told him "Cleveland." He said, "Do you want to read something?" Duck Hill, Mississippi, was a town right up the road. And they had a hanging tree there where they had just lynched a colored guy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And so first time we went to town we saw the hanging tree, and that's right in the middle of the town there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: In fact, there was really nothing to do there. And somewhere along the line spinal meningitis broke out in the camp. And it was about -- I bet you it was three months before we ever went to town, ever got out of the camp on account of the spinal meningitis. And we were frozen, and we trained in that. And from -- I forget how many months we were there. Then we left there, and we went to maneuvers in the mountains of Tennessee for three months in the wintertime. And this was real life for the Army. You live in a hole, and you lived out in the elements. And I remember Christmas day it rained like hell all day long, and our Christmas dinner was a piece of turkey with something. By the time we got to the tent, it was all soup. And we spent the whole day playing blackjack in the tent. So from there after the maneuver we got a -- we got a furlough to come home. And it was the wintertime, February. And after being in the mountains, living outside, I came home to Cleveland. And the first time I'd been in a bed for three months because in infantry division, you spend more time out in the field than you do in the barracks even. So when you go out there and spend many a night in the field, and your barrack is back there. So anyway, I came home on a furlough, and I felt like going out to sleep on the porch. I was uncomfortable because I'd been outside for three months, never inside to sleep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So when the furlough is over, I had to report back to Fort Jackson, South Carolina, which was a real nice camp. And we spent the rest of our time there. We got alerted two or three times. Fighting was going on in North Africa. They hadn't invaded Europe yet. And every once in a while we got alerted. And then all of a sudden they pulled maybe a hundred people out from different units in the division to ship them to North Africa to replace those people getting killed in that. And then it was all kind of things going on at that time. They'd close up like the artillery down in the Panama Canal zone. It became obsolete, and they'd pull that outfit. And all of a sudden they would pull them in with you, and you'd have to kind of retrain. They'd been in the service longer, and a lot of them were sergeants and corporals and that, and rank was frozen. And rank is hard to get in an infantry division because there's so many people, private, PFC, and you get to -- I got to be a corporal, fortunately. It was considered the best rank in the service because you had enough to get out of -- you did no KP, and the only thing you did was a corporal, the guard, or that. Where the poor private, the PFC did everything. And so we got many replacements and ASTP, Panama Canal zone. And so many of these guys come into the Panama Canal zone, they had malaria, a lot of malaria. And we got alerted two or three times. And finally we shoved off for Camp Kilmer, New Jersey, and stayed there for a week. And luckily, I got to come home from New York before I left. I couldn't tell anybody. And of course I didn't know where I was going either. And so we spent 12 days at Camp Kilmer, New Jersey. And never knew New York was not a deep water port. We loaded up on a Friday night and a funny feeling. You think you're serving your country, but you come from the New Jersey side to board the ship and the band playing when you got there and everything, coffee and doughnuts and everything. But over at the gates to get out on the street there was guys with machine guns there, MPs with constant submachine guns. So you either went up the gangplank or you jumped in the water or you hit the gate if you wanted. So you get a funny feeling. You know, you think you're serving your country, but you had no choice but to go up that gangplank. So the ship we went over on -- our ship -- some of the guys went on the Queen Mary and Elizabeth. They were the luxury ships. But this -- went over on a ship, the Louis Pasteur, and it was a French ship with a British crew, British Merchant Marine. And they were using that to bring prisoners back and troops over. And the whole interior of the ship was tore out and the cabins, and they had barbwire emplacements there -- actually boxed off. And the only difference between us and the prisoners is the gate was left open. And they have it in sections maybe twice the size of this room. No bunks or anything. Some of us had a mattress on the floor. Some of us had a hammock. And anyway, we was supposed to leave New York about midnight or something. And we missed a tide, which didn't realize that the tide was important in New York. So we didn't leave until 2 or 3 o'clock the next afternoon. Foggy, and we were out there. They issued us all life jackets. We had our clothes on all the time across nine days, life jackets, clothes. Take your shoes off only. Got one shower in nine days, salt water shower. Couldn't clean up. But anyway the first night out, the ship stopped. What's going on? Crew members and the submarines out there. This is -- this is a real, real taste of the real world, you know, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in a convoy or were you going --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. No. The big ship was too fast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Too fast for a convoy, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: The only time we had convoys was when we left England. But anyway we -- a ship could actually go in about six days. But on account of zigzagging around, the northern route of Newfoundland is the shortest route. So we took off from there from New York. And I guess the same thing happened up there. And then they went south, and we crossed the Azores. Where are you going? We assume you are going to England. So about a day out of -- half a day out of England we see a boat come out. You see planes circling around, and here is a pilot to take us to the mine fields going into England. And this old gentleman who is a pilot, they had to help him up the rope ladder to get in. And we thought, "Holy mackerel, we're in trouble. He's going to take us to the mine fields? I don't think he can see even." But he took us into Liverpool. That's where we landed, in Liverpool. And were at Liverpool 13 days, I think. And from Liverpool we -- Liverpool they took us into a town called Macclesfield. And half of the division was in Scotland, which we didn't know, and half of us in England because the main body of the division stands -- landed in Scotland. And of course Liverpool was north where it was away from the air raids. So we traveled by night only going down. We were there for 13 days before we hit the convoy to go to France.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. So this would be during the summer of '44 sometime?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: In the wintertime.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Winter of '44?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. So this was late?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you actually land in France?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Rouen, the mouth of the river in the Rouen. It's a little bit north or a little higher.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the convoy over --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: The war was already --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: November, December was when you were -- not convoy, but when you went over.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Right. Right. And we went over. And it was -- actually, we were on the channel about three days. We loaded up air balloons and -- to keep the convoys away. I mean, the air raids away.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And then when we -- we got to France, the war was already up into France so we landed at Rouen. And then from then on it was truck until we got up into the Metz area, and that was the first combat in Metz. We helped take the town of Metz with the fifth division. And we -- that's where we first went into battle, and that's where we were at when the Battle of the Bulge started.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of combat?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: At Metz.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Personally, though, do you remember your -- what you felt that day?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Scared shitless. No heroes. Of course the infantry, the riflemen, they caught the brunt of everything. They were more casualties than anybody. And I was -- I was in a -- in an artillery outfit, and I was a wire man with the artillery and worked with the infantry when they needed power, firepower to protect them or knock the enemy off of them. It was our job in communications. At that time there was very little radio used because the Germans could pick up the radio and know exactly what you was doing. So we actually strung wires between the artillery and the infantry, and they needed support. You telephone back to the artillery what to do. And so we spent a lot of time with -- in the wire section. We spent more time with the infantry than -- than the artillery guys did because they were cannoneers, the firepower. And then our division, -- all the infantry division was four battalions of artillery. And three of them are 105 outfits that support the three regiments, that each infantry division has three regiments. And the 155 outfit is general support of all so they can't hit us. We had more range than they did. And we had more -- more firepower than they did because of more explosives. So any tanks -- when we crossed the Rhein, we crossed the -- we got a nickname of Big Jack's Mortal Battalion because we crossed with the infantry, and we -- our guns would shoot 11 miles for chrissake.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So anyway then we went all the way to Czechoslovakia.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you actually were stringing wire? Was that part of your job?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well, yeah, yeah. We had a cable between -- back at the -- back at the artillery you had a switchboard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And from the switchboard you had a line to east gun.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: You had a gun back to the battalion, and you had a line to the division. And then they had a fire direction center that called back. And actually, our guys, we would be with the infantry, and you'd be on the telephone. And some officer would say, well, Jesus Christ, they are breaking through over there or something. So you'd give them coordinates and call back, and the guns didn't make adjustments. And they'd say, oh, say, a certain shell, HE, was high explosive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: (Go) smoke, high burst, where some of them went off in the air. They were time fuses where they went off in other ones. If you are going to shoot at a tank or something, then it would be high explosive where you'd actually hit the tank or close by. So these were -- and they had all different type of fuses they come out with. They'd call it a prosit (ph) where they would go off. And if there was troops there, they would automatically go off, and this is something that came later on in the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So we were close. They were all 87th Division.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And of course there was other units out there too, you know, and so -- but basically that's what my job was, was a wire man with the artillery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were stringing the wire, was there anything that you could do to hide it or protect it from being cut?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. See, well, this was a big thing. What was happening so much of the war, especially where a tank was used, and that was basically along the highways due to the fact of mud and this and that. And of course infantry spread out all over, to moving everything was basically along the highways and you'd go across the fields and all that, but the roads were very important. And of course being on an offensive unit, we didn't know what was up the road where the Germans were retreating all -- not all the time, but basically. And I know when we got -- when I say retreating, when we moved up to -- we were not getting ahead of ourself or behind, I don't know. When we got up to the Bulge from the southern part up there, the first time we got in action at the Bulge, we had three batteries, A, B, and C. And we're stringing wire to different units, and we're shooting in this direction. And one of our batteries is shooting in this direction, and one is over here. We're damn-near surrounded. So you think the war is one line here. It's not that way. So it's -- the infantry boys is the guy that caught hell. They were face to face all the time. Where we were with them, but we were maybe one day with them and then back another day or the radio operator. They started with the radio because a lot of times your guns would be two miles from where you were, and you had to string wire there. And to answer your question, the shells would knock it out. And then at the Bulge it was a dangerous deal because some of the tricks that they did. They would come and cut your line and maybe wait for you to come to fix it because they knew somebody is going to come along to fix it. And sometimes they'd just take and put a needle or something in there to short circuit it. You didn't know where the hell it was at. So you had to go and clip in. You could call back here and there. So there was a -- the Bulge was a different type of warfare because they had -- there was some of their own troops to, you know, camp. American uniforms, and they'd get on and they'd talk and everything American English, and it took a long time to, you know, straighten things out because -- so the war wasn't -- it was a different deal. The war wasn't always fighting up front because they are great with pincer movements to get behind you. And this is exactly what they did to you. They were fighting -- some rear echelon and troops, a quarter master and everything else that was not really trained to fight. They were fighting, if you seen some of the movies, because it just wasn't a front-line affair.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did your outfit encounter any of the infiltrators?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did your outfit encounter any of the infiltrators, those coming in in American uniforms?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. I'd say, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not particularly?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Not me personally. I'm sure some of the -- some of the deal was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think we got it on tape that your unit was in the SAR region?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Sarabella, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell that again so we get it on tape.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: The march up there was in freezing weather. We had a lot of casualties, trucks off the road. And it was so cold riding in the trucks and that, that when you'd jump off the truck to take a breather, take a break and relieve yourself, you'd just collapse. You had no feelings in your legs, you know. It was just colder than hell, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what happened next? Do you have any other particular memories of the Bulge, first of all?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Other than I think we had as many casualties from the weather, and we lived off the land more than we -- we didn't get fed. I mean, believe me. Stealing chickens, stealing eggs. And nobody got fat over there, believe me. And of course after the Bulge, things would change a little bit. But there was people got frozen feet and that. I know I got some frostbite on my toes, and it's just never the same. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that a problem with supplying you guys as far as not getting fed, or did they want you to live off the land?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. No. No. The thing is -- what happened, the farther -- you are moving pretty fast and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: -- and the farther up you got the worse it got. I know people that -- friends of mine that were back in France and that never missed a meal, three days a meal -- three meals a day. And never slept outside or anything else. So in an infantry division, once you start to move and that, you just can't keep up with it. And the trucks get blown up and that, too. So I know one night there was a scary night that -- what would happen, before we moved the guns, there would be some of us in the wire section, wire section basically and maybe one gun sheath. You would go off to fix it. Pick a spot where you're going to put the guns in so you'd have some idea with -- and in the wire section and my section there was about 14 of us. The radio section had another 14, maybe. And so we'd take turns on doing some of these things. And one night we went out there. We had a fresh officer with us, second lieutenant. Where he came from, I don't know. And they said take him along. He was helpless, worthless. And anyway we went -- got a radio message to stay there. The guns had a -- had to -- a fire emission, and hold there until further notice. We're out in no-man's land, by ourself, four or five of us. And said dig in because you're going to be there all night long. And one of the most embarrassing things, we all dug in. And somebody crawled out of this hole and put a candle down there, whatever, to keep warm. And one guy come out and he says, "I see something moving around on the hill up there." We all jump out. I had shoes -- one shoe off, I think, and jumped out in the damn snow. Sure enough, the thing is moving up there. So we decided to -- let's go up there and see what it was. We start firing. And I said switch from the M1 to a hard beam. And I go to hit the safety and the goddamn clip fell out in the snow. Here I got one shoe off, and I can't find ammunition for my gun even. So these are things that -- you are a soldier, but you're scared shitless half of the time. So that was one -- one case. And another night we were the same thing, out in the coldest to hold. We went to go -- and they said go ahead on up the road, and they gave us coordinates on the map where we should go. We went to go around the corner of the road, and there was a tagger royal tank sitting, and he had the muzzle right down the road waiting for something to come around. They must have been sleeping because they didn't fire on us, and we pulled back. Got on the radio. They said, stay there. So we stayed there all night long. And we heard the -- the tank start up a couple of times, and nobody wanted to go and take a look because right around the corner he had the muzzle. So to show you some of the stupid things guys will do even in -- when it comes to danger, right across the street was a farmhouse -- a road. We're kind of in the ditch and the road -- a farmhouse there. And in the morning it got daylight. Some farmer brings a -- they had a track to bring manure out of the barn, bring it out. And the little girl's with him, and they dump it, and the steam comes off of the damn crap. And they go back in for another load and somebody said -- we had different canisters with different colored smoke to mark targets. Somebody said, Gee, whiz. Wouldn't it be something if we threw one of the smoke bombs over there to -- these are blue, pink and beautiful. And we shouldn't have done this, but somebody got the canister and threw it over in that manure pile. And all of a sudden a pink smoke started to come out of the manure pile. And the little girl come out and saw this. She didn't see us. They didn't even know we were there. Seen this goddamn smoke coming off of there, the steam, beautiful pink smoke or blue or whatever it was. She runs in and gets her father or grandfather. And he comes out, and he says, "Ha, what's that? What the heck happened here?" And all of a sudden the tank starts up. We didn't even know it was there. The second lieutenant was with us said, "Oh, my God. We're in trouble now." And we didn't know it, but we scared the tank off because he saw that and he thought he was being marked for a target, and he took off in the other direction.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And it was stupid on our part. But anyway, we survived it, so. This was the kind of stuff that went on, and you wonder why you survive sometimes so. So I don't know what else I can tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of buddies you want to tell me about?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: The best buddies I ever had, and some of them I knew better than my own relation. You are together for over three years. You slept together, fought together, got drunk together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. And I -- we have a -- we used to have a -- you know, where 87th Division -- Highway 87 is off --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: That was dedicated to the 87th Division.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, I didn't realize that.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: We used to have a chapter in Cleveland here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And we still have the division reunion every year. And our chapter in Cleveland here was several fellows, and we get together, picnics, and everything else. And that kind of deteriorated, and some of the guys died off and moved away. And then there's the national division, which we used to have the 87th National Division in Cleveland here. We had it here twice. And that's when we put that sign up out there, the 87th Division, Highway 87.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: The acorn, that's 322.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, 322 is dedicated to the 87th?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: I think it is.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: I think it's 322. And anyway, it narrows down. We have a battery reunion, which SWO (ph) posted it. And we had that every year for a while. Now it's down to every other year. And so last year -- actually what happens is we go to the reunions, and there's more widows and grandkids in there than there are members.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So after the Bulge, where did you -- where did you go next?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: We went clear to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Get that map out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There was no more --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, no. The war didn't end there. I mean, there was a helluva lot of fighting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What else -- what other combat memories do you have after the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Reached the Siegfried line in February of '45.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah. And we wound up clear in Pilson, Czechoslovakia. But this was all constant war, and of course this is different. You are taking a lot of prisoners there. And we had casualties and people getting killed. I mean, it didn't end in the Battle of the Bulge. And that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you stopped --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: One of the movies that they showed about Germans throwing down their arms and marching back to Germany, well, that was boloney. They was still fighting of the -- but you got more involved with inexperienced troops maybe and because the war -- the Germans was still fighting the Russians, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When -- you went to Pilson, right? Pilson, Czechoslovakia?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you encounter any POWs when you were in Pilson?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: American POWs?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: All along the road we were picking them up here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were picking up American GIs and stuff like this?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And not only them, but Polish.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Polish?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Slave labor and this and that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: We had a lot of trouble with them in some places because they wanted to go burn the farmers' barns down and everything else. And -- and a lot of those people they -- some of these stories you hear about some of these guys that -- this one guy who lives out here that they want to deport and that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: It's hard to tell because when you -- you do a lot of things that you are told to do. You are not always proud of what you do, you know, and maybe he went overboard. I have no idea; I wasn't there. But I saw people shot that shouldn't have been shot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: But you're scared.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And I know I've seen a couple times that some of our own soldiers overdid their shooting. I mean, if a prisoner was -- I saw a bunch of prisoners lined up one time. And a guy went to make a move to release his belt, a gun belt or something. And he not only shoot him once, he unloaded a whole clip on him. And these are things that -- these things do happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: You are scared. Everybody got a gun, and it's something that's -- you don't know what you're going to do unless you're there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, the reason I'm asking you about Pilson, I'd like to believe some day I'm going to meet this guy or these guys. Because my dad, the prison camp that he ended up in was here in Chemnitz.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: At Chemnitz?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: That town, I remember that town real well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you go to there? You went there?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah. That was great for instruments. They built -- the shops were filled with accordions, saxophones, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I keep talking to these guys, I wonder if any of these guys ever met my dad.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of course, but --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: -- could be.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But wouldn't that be interesting?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well, Chemnitz, I remembered it real well because it was noted for -- here is where we crossed the Rhine here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And they had -- they were building, working on -- well, one of many -- underground missile factories there near that camp, maybe about ten miles away from that camp.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: These were things that went on, and there were so many things happened. We had one guy in our unit -- not our unit but in the division. Honestly, to answer your questions, I would have to say no because every day you'd meet guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Here is what you saw in some of those.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But if you specifically remembered seeing a scrawny American POW, that would have been amazing.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well, they all looked --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They all looked that way, I know.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Here is a true picture of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And here is a true picture of Patton, you know, not what you see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever meet Patton or get close to him?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: I saw him twice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't get a chance to --

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. We were two different levels. I was a corporal. This -- I saw him twice. And he was -- as a matter of fact I -- I could have almost been in the picture on one of these here history --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A documentary on the History Channel?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: -- where Patton was talking to one of -- we had three generals in that division. One major general and two brigadier generals. And he was giving our artillery officer some yakking here, and he was probably from here to the street out there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: I saw him twice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: But he would have told me to get the hell out of the way probably. No. But this is -- this is a history, and this is all the units.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: This is New York. And right from day one the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about mail call? Getting letters from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Not all the time because v-mail was a real popular -- sending letters out. The only thing we could -- we were limited to what we could say, what country you were in: "I'm okay." You couldn't describe anything else. Some people had codes with their girlfriends. I saw Johnny yesterday or something, but I didn't. But no. Once -- once we left England, it was strictly v-mail. And you could tell -- you couldn't talk about the weather. "I'm okay." You couldn't tell what country you were in. And there was -- you couldn't -- you couldn't say anything. They were all -- somebody read them before. They were all read by an officer before they was shipped out, so it was mostly just v-mail, a couple lines. Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about the letters you got from the United States?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Okay. Well, I tell you, there was a lot of stuff lost. You know, you moved. As a matter of fact, when we got overseas, we used to have a barracks bag, a little bit different than what we got discharged with. When we got overseas, every unit was different. Once we left, I had a -- a silver dollar that my dad gave me with my serial number on it. And I had it in England. They got rid of that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: You wasn't -- no cameras or anything. Some people always snuck stuff around, you know, but -- END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: When we -- we had two bags when we left England. One with our everyday stuff and one with, like, shoes and some personal dress stuff that you don't need.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And they was supposed to -- this was personal belongings, and the B bag was supposed to be left back in France. Well, we never saw them again. Whether they were captured or somebody robbed them or this, so any personal. As a matter of fact, anything with identification with your home address, you wasn't supposed to have. So in case you were captured, I guess prisoners of war, there was a hell of a lot of stuff that -- that would give any information so they would write home or this. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: But that never affected me. But things changed after we left England.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Is that still running?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. It sure is.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, is it? Oh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It's still running. When you think about that whole experience over there, is there any one particular vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: There's something I'm very happy and proud I took part of and times I was -- wish I'd have been home, but I would have been disappointed if I hadn't participated with knowing what goes on now. And I think it's a disgrace that people don't back the veterans a little bit more. And even today, with the war going on over there, people just don't know. They are used to TV and this and that, and they think there's too much glamour to it. There's no glamour to it. You know, it -- it isn't in a person to kill another person. And I know this is one thing in basic training, they used to show us films. "You have every man in your sight. He's got you in his sight. And if you don't pull the trigger, he's going to pull the trigger." So it's -- and I saw certain things I had nothing to do. But certain things I saw that went on, and it was not -- it was not right. One incident that I remember that, some place during the Battle of the Bulge, the graves registration used to come up, and that was their job, to pick up the dead. And they'd pick up the dead Germans and the Americans both, and a lot of them were just like cord wood, frozen, you know. And I think there were a hell of a lot of casualties up there. People would have been living today if they would have been in warm weather because it was so cold. Once they lost blood, they died, and they'd be frozen like a statue. And some quarter master outfit come up, and they start picking guys up and throwing them on the truck, same truck, and they just throw them on like cord wood. And one guy took some toilet paper. You used to keep toilet paper in your helmet and a pair of socks there maybe too to keep them dry. And he took some toilet paper, and he took it, and he shoved it in the German's hand. It was froze, and he threw him on the truck. And one buddy from Arkansas, which I talk to quite frequently, he went over and he said, "What the hell did you do that for?" And he said, "When we take them back, I want to tell the guys we got the German with his pants down, and we shot him." And this guy says, "If I see you do it again, I'll shoot you because you still respect the dead, you know." And he meant it. And this guy thought it was some smart-aleck affair, but he was not a combat soldier. He was just picking up the dead. So these are things that, I'm sure, went on. And war's no joke. But this guy talking and this fellow I talked to, he wound up in the Korean war too, so. I -- I almost -- if I -- this fellow I'm talking about, him and I joined the Reserves at the same time. After the war come along we do something that, something we knew what we were doing, and I never went to any meetings here. I didn't have to because I was "inactive reserve." He lived in a small town in Arkansas -- [cough] small town in Arkansas, and he got called up in the Korean War. And he said, "What the hell." And how he got called up, he went over one night to a meeting where you go to the armory just to see what was going on, and they told him to sign in. And he signed in, and then a couple months later he gets a check for a couple bucks. And he thought, well, this must be back pay or something. He got two checks, and the Korean war come along. They called him up. He spent a year over there because he signed that paper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah, but I still talk to some of those guys. Every time I see these movies, they bring back memories. Sometimes they glamorize the war too much, and it's no picnic.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And -- and I don't think -- I don't know what happens now, but the farther you got up, the less you got to eat. Your clothing, just like I got my galoshes off a dead guy over there. I was never proud of that, but we just had regular shoes, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And some of the guys coming over as replacements, they'd have a better type of shoes than we had, galoshes and that. And this guy I'm talking about, he says, "Singleton," he says, "I think those would fit you." And I took them off that dead guy and put them on my own feet. I said it's part of life. I mean, he didn't need them. And you think of that being cruel, but it's a matter of survival. And the same thing as far as -- I don't know if they could do any better or not, but we sure as hell didn't get a lot to eat so. And the farther back you were, the better it was so. And of course the infantry got it a hell of a lot worse than we did so because they -- somebody shooting at them all the time. They had more casualties than anybody. So I don't know what else I can tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Once you were in Germany, and the German people realized that you weren't the monsters that their propaganda said you were, were they pretty nice to you?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They -- getting to the things that happen, you don't know who to trust. We were -- what would happen, we'd take over a village. And you couldn't -- didn't know what these people were going to do because what would happen is somewhere along the line these -- Hitler used -- which was like a Boy Scout. They used to train those kids to -- they'd leave things behind them to do damage. Blow trucks and that up at night. And they had what they called the Pander Puff, which was equivalent to our Bazooka. And they would shoot them once, and they were no good. Where a Bazooka was like a piece of pipe, and you'd put the rocket in and put a wire around it for the batteries to charge it. Pull the trigger, it would shoot off. But you kept -- you used the same thing all the time. Where the Pander Puff -- once you shot it, it was no good. And they used to leave those behind with the kids. And they'd blow trucks up, tanks at night, and they'd wind up getting shot, you know, and these were 12-year-old kids. And another time where we used to -- if you took over a village, you'd take all the civilians that was left behind, usually old men or old women or young people. You'd put them in three or four houses in the village. And then every once in a while they would let, if they had livestock and that, they'd let them go back to -- to, you know, feed them or whatever. And one of our units was down the road from us in the houses. We'd stay in the houses sometime and -- if we could. And some woman used to come down the street and wave at the guys all the time. It took them about two days to get used to that. But they got them houses she would wave at would get shelled. And some spotter someplace would see this woman -- wherever she'd wave, she was marking a target where people were in those houses. And then after she walked down the street, the house would get shelled. So they wound up shooting that woman so -- and dogs the same way. There was times that they had dogs trained to come, and then at nighttime they would go back and get a patrol to come up through. The dogs knew where you were at. So certain times you'd shoot dogs. So these are things that changes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So. And I ran across a situation a while back, a girl that worked in the office, her mother was in the Belgium underground. And this girl was born in Belgium and her parents moved here. Her -- it just so happened her -- her mother married an American officer. They came to this country after the war. And she asked me, she said some of my relations are coming over to visit, and I'd like to have you come over to the house and meet some of these people from Belgium. They'd like to talk to you. I said, oh, a conversation, where are you at and this and that. And I says, "I remember some of the houses we were in. The Germans had been there first, and they'd build a fire in every room of the house and burn furniture to keep warm." And she said, "Well, some of the Americans did it, too." And it was kind of embarrassing. It wasn't me. Because in one house -- we were in Belgium -- the only ones that was left behind usually was old people, sick people. And there was an old man that was in this house, and he was sick. And we were there for two or three days. And we shaved that guy up, anybody had any shaving lotion. They powdered him up, and we'd have to give him a little soup or something. And after we were there a couple, three days, and we'd move out. They both cried. They said the "bosh" is coming and they'd burn furniture in their house. We said, no, the "bosh" is not coming. They are well up the road. And -- and so I remember those old people, but I remember about burning their house. You know, they said the Americans did the same thing, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think we recorded -- we were talking about before we started the tape -- the differences between fighting in France and fighting in Germany, the villages.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me that again so we get that recorded.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, in France, if the civilians -- they did anything for you. They want it paid for or they'd steal from you. If you parked your truck someplace for too long, you'd find some kids trying to unload it. And flashlight batteries was a big, big priority. And I don't know if I want this on tape or not, but one kid wanted to trade a couple flashlight batteries to sleep with his mother. So this -- this happened. I wasn't sleeping with his mother, though, believe me. But then once you got, like I say, into Germany and the people actually treated you better than the French did. I don't remember them trying to steal anything from us and not trading batteries for their mother either, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you were saying in France they would just level the villages. Both sides didn't care as much. Whereas in Germany, they were trying to preserve the villages?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah. What would happen is, see, when you were fighting in France and all the countries, Belgium, Luxembourg, and all of them, when they'd shell the place, they didn't care about whether they was blowing the buildings up or not. So what I'm saying, in those countries you were better off out in the open field away from any structure because they'd just shell it, and they figured you're there, and somebody is going to get killed. So once you got into Germany, you were safer in the village than you were out in the field sometimes. We weren't supposed to go in the houses, but a lot of times we did. So that was a difference. And of course you can -- you can understand that they didn't want to kill their own people. They knew there would be people in there, in the basements or whatever. So there was -- the war changed, and of course they are protecting their homeland. So and before -- once you got up near Czechoslovakia and that, that it was different. But there was a lot of slave camp -- a lot of camps up in that area. Slave they had -- some of these people, they had the Polish people and that in camps that would live in a barracks. And then all the German civilians that would have gone to war and that and then the farmer boys and that, they would come and work for the Germans and that. And some of the Germans are very abusive because after the war was over, some of these people wanted to go burn their houses and barns and slaughter them, you know, because they were punished. And so it was, you were kind of fighting -- not fighting them, but you were trying to -- and it's funny. You can't believe it, and the same thing is happening over there. We're going to pay for that war over there, which we paid to rebuild Germany. And the last stages of the war, it was a different kind of war. You kind of fought more on the open land than you did in the villages because you didn't want to -- the Germans would retreat in the houses and that, and you didn't want to blow that house up unless you had to. Because somebody is going to pay for it, and I guess we paid for it dearly with the Marshall Plan and that, I guess, so. But these are things that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: I -- I don't know what else to tell you other than --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, if you think you've covered it. Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your homecoming when you finally got home?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah. Well, when I first came -- yeah. My -- it's a little bit different for me. I was the last of 11 kids. And I don't remember my parents being young. My mother was 45 years old when I was born. So when I was in the service, they were in their 60s. Coming home I was happy to come home, but it wasn't no big crowd to greet me or anything. My brother picked me up at the station downtown and that. I mean, it was -- it was nice to get home. I mean, in the street there was no big parties or anything and because I -- we still had to go back, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So because I was in the service another four or five months after I came home from Europe. I came home in July, and I was in until January, the following January.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a possibility that you would have been sent to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Oh, that was the idea. As a matter of fact, I almost wound up in the Pacific. When we were at Fort Benning, Georgia -- you see everything, when you come home -- I got to go pretty soon.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We're wrapping it up here.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: When we came home, the war was still on in the Pacific. When we got down to Fort Benning, Georgia, we were going to train there. And I was back -- the outfit didn't come back at the same time because you actually had 30 days at home. So guys that lived in California and that, they were gone the next few weeks or ten days because travel was so different from New York to landing in. We -- coming back -- I didn't tell you -- we come in at Hampton Roads, Virginia, and wound up in -- one day at Hampton Roads. They gave us a service meal there with one coupon. The Germans served us. There was prisoners of war in this country, and they served us a welcome home meal where you could have a quart of milk and steak and all that stuff. And then from there, we had to go to -- I went to Atterbury, Indiana, to come home because everybody is going in different directions. That was not a discharge. That was just coming home from there. And anyway, I'm checked in at Fort Benning, and a guy come and woke me up, and he said, "Singleton, 641 Wire Chief." That was my -- he said, "You're going to report to the battalion. You're going to join the 95th division there, Camp Shelby, Mississippi. You're going over as a replacement." I said, "What the hell do you mean?" He says, "Yeah." So anyway, report to battalion, 8 o'clock in the morning. So what the hell is this? So that night I got woke up the second time by my battalion commander which had come back, and he was a lieutenant colonel, and I was one of the original guys in the outfit. And he said, "I understand that you have to join the 95th division as a replacement." And I said, "Yeah." And he says, "How do you feel about it?" I said, "Well, I'm not too happy about it, but I'd rather stick with you." He says, "Do you want to go in the hospital?" He says, "Are you sick or anything?" And he was giving me an out to go in the hospital. I said, "No, I don't want to go to no hospital." He said, "Well, I'm kind of proud of you that you are a soldier, and you go where you are told to go." So the next morning I go down to the battalion. And they start calling off names, and I see guys there. I knew I had been in the service longer than them, the same spec number I had. They called names. They didn't call mine, so I didn't get on the truck. The truck left and when the guy says, "You'll become a replacement. Somebody came back that had less time in than you." They had point systems. So I wound up -- I found out later the guys that went, they got on the ship to go over, halfway across when they dropped the bomb, and they turned around and come back. So I'd have been on that boat ride, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you got back?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. At that time it wouldn't have took too much for me to be a professional soldier. And of course I got -- this is once I got involved in the reserves, I was -- they kept sending me notices to come to meetings, and I never went because I found that the girls were fine, too, you know. So -- so that -- when it come time for my discharge, I took it, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Well, you know, it's kind of cruel, some of the replacements that came that -- I never forget that. When we had a replacement come just before we was going to cross the Mozelle River. And these guys had been in the service about three months where we had been in the service almost two years. And some of them, they just were not trained. They gave them a uniform and a gun, and they sent them over there to replacement. And some of them had never slept on the ground. They just didn't know how to take care of themself, and they came with better equipment. We had to have sleeping bags and better shoes and everything because they were fresh out of the states.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: And we were ready to go across the Mozelle River in the afternoon, and we got pushed back, and we were going to go the next morning. And this one replacement, a kid from Chicago -- I don't even remember his name -- first sergeant came around. We're all scattered around in the woods says, "Everybody ready to go?" And I said, "Well, that one guy he's in the damn sleeping bag and farting around, you know." And he said, "Well, get him out of there. Dump him." They kicked him, "Come on, kid. Get up." And I don't know what the hell he was doing. And he said, "Dump him." So he pulled the zipper down, and we actually dumped him out like a couple -- out of a potato sack, and he was trying to put his clothes on. And he said, "You don't take your clothes off over here." He had his pants off like he was taking a break. And the son of a bitch, you know. And here's a kid, I don't know his name. And after we crossed the river, we got shelled pretty good, and a lot of our lines was out. Blowing the lines up from the guns to the infantry, and the wire sectioner was one sergeant, two corporals, and the rest were privates, PFCs. Well, I was one of the corporals. And they had -- I had it pretty easy that day. And the sergeant come over, and I told him a line was out. And he says, "Well, pick a guy out to go fix it." And I said, "Shit, I had it hard all day." And he said, "Well, we all had it hard." I said, "I'll go." He said, "Okay. If you're going to go, go." He said, "Pick a man out." So I picked this guy out that I had dumped out of the sack, and he's supposed to be protecting me. You're operating in the dark because you know where your line is at, and sometimes you just grab them by hand and follow them and you don't know who the hell is out there, you know. And he's supposed to be protecting me because one guy was a rifle, and -- and that damn shell would go off from here up to the corner, which was nothing. He'd hit the dirt and, "Boy, that's close." I said, "Come on." So he's on his goddamn belly half of the night, and he's supposed to be protecting me. And he said, "That's close." I said, "No. We'll get a little closer than that." So I had him all night long, and we got back with the group. He said, "Boy, we had it tough last night. Boy, that's close." And, shit, I can go to asleep with the shells going off at the corner. But those were experienced guys, you know. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: So, anyway --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you got a lot of guys -- as the Bulge progressed, there were a lot of the guys with absolutely no experience, huh?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. Well, like I say, we were -- fortunately, we had been in the service a while. So, and those replacements, the division was just loaded with them. And especially in the infantry company. Christ, they lose 20 guys a day, you know. And that Ed Stock, he was a replacement. He was playing basketball in some college, I think, when they said, "Come on, you're going overseas." And they gave him a gun, and he didn't have the experience we had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not a whole lot of training?

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. He got wounded. He wound up someplace. I forget, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Singleton
sp.p: No. A lot of guys you'd never get to know their name even, so.
